papers_read.title_as_printed: Cross-lingual detection of mild cognitive impairment based on temporal parameters of spontaneous speech (Gosztolya et al., Computer Speech & Language 69 (2021) 101215)
Linguistic-based Mild Cognitive Impairment detection using Informative Loss (Pourramezan Fard, Mahoor, Alsuhaibani, Dodge; Computers in Biology and Medicine 176 (2024) 108606)

what_each_reports.P-58: SVM on 15 ASR-derived temporal speech parameters (articulation rate, tempo, silent/filled pause measures) from a telephone monologue about the previous day; 33 English speakers (New York; 19 HC, 14 MCI) and 33 Hungarian speakers (Szeged; 20 HC, 13 MCI), Petersen criteria, speaker-wise leave-one-out CV with nested tuning, metrics at equal error rate. 'All features' monolingual: English accuracy 84.8%, AUC 0.932; Hungarian accuracy 75.8%, AUC 0.727; feature-subset and cross-lingual scores span the abstract's '67-92%'.
what_each_reports.P-6: Transformer (sentence-embedding + sentence cross-attention) with InfoLoss on ASR transcripts of I-CONECT video-chat interviews, 68 participants aged 75+ (34 MCI, 34 NC; Portland and Detroit), subject-level 5-fold CV: accuracy 85.16% (SD 5.76), AUC 84.75% (SD 5.97); over five repeated fold configurations, mean AUC 79.94%.

quantity_a: Speaker-wise LOO-CV classification scores (accuracy, AUC and others at EER) for MCI vs HC from acoustic temporal/pause parameters of spontaneous telephone speech, in two 33-person English and Hungarian clinic samples.
quantity_b: Subject-level 5-fold CV accuracy/AUC for MCI vs NC from the semantic content of ASR transcripts of semi-structured video conversations, in the 68-person I-CONECT trial sample.
incompatible_if_same: No. P-6's 85.16% lies inside P-58's reported 67-92% range and almost equals P-58's English all-features accuracy of 84.8%. There is no disagreement even on the record's own numbers.

gates.task: match: both MCI vs cognitively normal detection (T1). P-6's registry Task_Type T2 looks wrong; the paper is MCI vs NC detection.
gates.dataset_family: mismatch: P-58 uses its own New York and Szeged clinic samples; P-6 uses I-CONECT (Portland/Detroit). The record's 'dataset_equal: Yes' is wrong; no waiver.
gates.validation_tier: match: internal cross-validation only in both.
gates.modality_family: match at family level (speech), but different channels: acoustic timing and pauses (P-58) vs transcript semantics (P-6).

endpoint_and_metric: compatible metric types (both report accuracy and AUC); the P-58 '67-92%' is a range spanning several metrics and feature subsets, not a single estimate.
performance_validity: flag does not apply: no contested figure is at or above 0.97.
independence: Distinct studies, cohorts and author groups.
grounds: P-6's 85.16% accuracy falls inside P-58's reported 67-92% range and matches P-58's English all-features accuracy (84.8%), so the two results describe no disagreement.
The record's 'P-58: 67-92% range' is a mixed-metric span across feature subsets, languages and ASR systems, not one estimate that could be set against 85.16%.
Different cohorts (dataset gate fails) and different speech channels (acoustic pauses vs transcript semantics) mean that even a gap would not be a conflict on one quantity.

record_defects: dataset_equal 'Yes' is wrong: P-58 uses New York and Szeged clinic samples, P-6 the I-CONECT trial.
The rejection reason 'Metric type unclear: Unknown / Acc' is inaccurate: P-58 reports accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1 and AUC per feature set; the '67-92%' is a range across them.
P-6 registry row has Task_Type T2 and Best_Metric AUC 0.8475, whereas the paper is MCI vs NC detection (T1); the record's T1 is right.
P-6 note (not in the record): Section 4.5 says 'our proposed framework achieved the AUC value of 85.16%', conflating its accuracy with its AUC (84.75%).
what_would_change_the_verdict: Nothing in these papers: the recorded figures agree. A conflict would need the same speech features evaluated on a shared cohort with non-overlapping results.
